architecture.orchestration: strict sequential pipeline with two gates: DRL window filter, then priority threshold before the LLM; human is final decision authority; the anomaly score is deliberately excluded from the DRL state to prevent feature leakage; pseudonymization applied before any LLM call with a reversible SOC-side placeholder mapping

datasets: BOSS of the SOC (BOTS) subset (~12k instances)
custom simulated corpus (300k instances, Kali -> Windows 11)
evaluation.reported_results: BOTS: mode B F1 0.861, recall 0.873; simulated corpus: mode D precision 0.926, recall 0.696, F1 0.795 with the lowest regret 1.358; ~63-65% reduction in traffic forwarded to the LLM

limitations: Fixed 5-minute windows can miss short-lived attacks
Binary action space (Allow/Contain) only; no monitor/throttle/escalate
No RAG or vector store; context management is funneling-only
No retry or fallback logic documented for LLM or SPL failures
Read-only by design; all mitigation executed by humans (intentional)
Dataset scale and diversity limited; single-attacker simulation
Local-LLM accuracy and hallucination risk untested

components.implementation: Zero-shot LLM agent with three structured actions: run_sql, submit_flags, and give_up; models accessed through LiteLLM; Section 4.4.

components.implementation: Ground truth is hidden from the hunter; Coverage Score is the instance-weighted fraction of coverable narrative steps surfaced; Sections 3.2 and 8.3.

components.role: score whether submitted evidence covers the attack narrative

memory.details: The current briefing, prior actions, latest query, and result/error are carried in the agent conversation state; no vector store or RAG memory is used.

architecture.orchestration: ReAct-like evidence-gathering loop: the LLM repeatedly chooses run_sql, observes up to 10 rows, updates its hypothesis in conversation history, and either queries again, submits candidate malicious timestamps, or gives up. Investigation is capped at 50 SQL queries and 75 total turns; the evaluator alone sees the hidden ground truth.

baselines: same zero-shot UniversalHunter prompt and query budget across evaluated frontier models
datasets: 500 synthetic benign Sysmon EventID-1 records per campaign
evaluation.reported_results: Technical Report v1 evaluates 859 hunt runs. Claude Opus 4.6 leads with Coverage Score 0.55±0.05 and 4.48%±1.40% malicious flags found; no model meets the paper's operational bar of >=50% recall on every ATT&CK tactic, and no model completes a hunt. The benchmark spans 106 procedures, 93 ATT&CK sub-techniques, and 12 tactics (Tables 2 and 5; Sections 8-9).

limitations: Several models are evaluated with a single rollout despite high LLM nondeterminism; the authors recommend multi-rollout averaging.
All attack telemetry is Windows-only; Linux auditd, cloud telemetry, and network-flow hunting are not covered.
Only 500 synthetic benign Sysmon EventID-1 records are injected, far below production SOC noise volume.
Exact timestamp matching is intentionally strict and does not award partial credit for coarse but useful investigative localization.
All evaluated hunters are zero-shot; trained or retrieval-augmented agents are outside this version's evaluation.
The campaign generator is proprietary, although pre-built campaign data and full hunt traces are released.

architecture.orchestration: plan-then-execute loop with a reasoning-tier planner and cheap executors; per-stage tool-call and token budgets; checkpointed replanning on failure; deterministic verification between agent output and tool execution; human approval gates for destructive actions; sandboxed containers

evaluation.reported_results: NYU CTF Bench 2026: Claude 4.5 Opus 59%, Gemini 3 Pro 52%, +9.5 points with a Kali tool environment; AIxCC finalists found 54/63 (86%) synthetic vulnerabilities and patched 43 (68%) across 54M LoC, plus 18 previously unknown real-world vulnerabilities; IRIS found 55 vs CodeQL 27; guided task-tree completion 71.8-78.6% vs 13.5-16.5% self-guided; AutoPT $0.024/test, RapidPen $0.30-0.60/test

limitations: CTF benchmarks do not equal production (authorization, rate limits, ambiguous success)
Hallucination documented: invented file paths, misread forms, inferred nonexistent control flow
Indirect prompt injection via untrusted page and log content; tool, memory, and RAG poisoning
Containment imperfect in practice (shared kernels, metadata services; Clinejection incident hit ~4,000 developers)
Context limits and lost-in-the-middle; retrieval failures can omit crucial evidence
Reasoning-class model costs 5-20x per token
Dual-use: scoped defensive prompts trivially repurposable

components.implementation: JSON/CSV harness released with deterministic stub mode; the paper explicitly labels it illustrative scaffolding rather than a validated production framework; Sections 6 and 10.
components.name: Evaluation harness
components.role: measure agent accuracy, latency, and prompt-injection susceptibility

memory.details: The paper discusses shared message buses and conversational context but does not specify one persistent memory mechanism for the reference implementation.

architecture.orchestration: Reference architecture supports a single-agent ReAct loop or a multi-agent coordinator using pipeline, debate, or blackboard patterns. Tool calls pass through typed registries and sanitization boundaries; high-risk actions can be gated by confidence thresholds and human approval. The authors explicitly state that the released implementation is illustrative scaffolding, not a validated production framework (Section 10).

baselines: deterministic stub on real Edge-IIoTset sample
evaluation.reported_results: The shipped validation run is a harness sanity check, not an LLM capability result: the deterministic stub reports F1 0.83 on synthetic traffic; a negative-control transfer drops accuracy from 0.78 on synthetic data to 0.06 on real Edge-IIoTset. The paper defers real-model production validation (Sections 2.4, 6, and 10.3).

limitations: The paper is a systematic survey plus reference scaffold, not one empirically validated end-to-end security architecture.
The shipped harness validation uses a deterministic stub rather than an LLM agent, so its scores cannot be treated as agent capability evidence.
The synthetic-to-real negative control shows a major generalization gap (0.78 to 0.06 accuracy).
Real-model evaluation across accuracy, latency, robustness, and prompt injection is deferred to staged future validation.
The survey literature is heterogeneous across datasets, attack taxonomies, and deployment assumptions, limiting direct quantitative comparison.

Prompt injection, data poisoning (1-5%), and poor confidence calibration remain exploitable
Benchmark-to-production gap; few longitudinal operational SOC deployments
Fine-tuning cost (tens of thousands of USD for GPT-3-class models) and RAG latency (2-5x)

architecture.orchestration: Fixed RAG pipeline: preprocess incident events -> embed events and query -> retrieve top-K matching events -> enrich context -> generate an answer with Llama 3.1 8B. Retrieval is a predetermined stage, so under the repository convention this is RAG rather than an agentic tool loop.

datasets: synthetic DFIR incident scenarios covering phishing, SYN-flood/network attacks, Windows-style events, and mixed incident timelines
evaluation.reported_results: The peer-reviewed version reports aggregate accuracy 95.52%, relevance 94.51%, exact match 100%, top-K 100%, and overall performance 97.51% under the authors' synthetic controlled scenarios (Section 5.3/Table 9). The paper cautions that the experimental configuration limits generalisability.

limitations: Evaluation uses synthetic, controlled incident scenarios rather than a production SOC or legal-forensics workload.
The authors state that GenDFIR should not be treated as a universal DFIR solution and that results may not generalize beyond the tested configuration.
Ground-truth checking and relevance assessment rely on a custom evaluation procedure rather than a broadly standardized DFIR benchmark.
RAG can ground answers in incident evidence but does not itself guarantee forensic provenance, chain of custody, or hallucination-free conclusions.
The fixed retrieval pipeline cannot autonomously decide to launch new telemetry queries when the retrieved context is insufficient.

memory.details: No persistent retrieval, graph, or episodic memory is used at inference time.

architecture.orchestration: Offline data preparation and supervised adaptation are followed by a fixed auditor -> verifier inference pipeline. The paper's contribution is weight adaptation (FFT/LoRA); inference does not use retrieval, external tools, or model-directed iterative actions, so it is classified as fine-tuned under the repository convention.

evaluation.reported_results: With ROS, Llama3 FFT reaches precision 0.84, recall 0.79, F1 0.83; Qwen2 FFT-ROS reaches precision 0.85, recall 0.80, F1 0.82. For token-price manipulation, Llama3 FFT reports precision 0.97 and recall 0.68. The paper also reports that prompt-only Qwen2 performs far worse (F1 0.20), supporting the value of domain fine-tuning.

limitations: The dataset is specific to Solidity/DApp security, so transfer to operating-system, network, or SOC threat-hunting telemetry is not established.
The key token-price-manipulation evaluation contains only 23 vulnerable contracts, limiting confidence for that rare logical-flaw class.
Random over-sampling duplicates minority examples and can increase overfitting risk even when it improves class balance.
The inference pipeline has no retrieval or external verification tool, so correctness remains dependent on the specialized model and verifier prompt.
LoRA is cheaper but underperforms full-parameter fine-tuning in the reported experiments, exposing an accuracy-versus-training-cost trade-off.
